paragraphs: Dear Sir or Madam,

I am writing in response to your article on the council's plan to replace part of Riverside Park with a car park for commuters. As a regular visitor to the park, I strongly object to this idea and would like to propose a better solution.

First and foremost, the park is the only green space within walking distance for thousands of residents of all ages. Young parents bring their children to the playground, one of the few safe places to play outdoors. Teenagers like me use the paths for jogging and cycling. For elderly people, a daily walk among the trees is often their main form of exercise and a chance to meet neighbours. Losing even part of the park would therefore affect almost everyone.

The council should instead consider building a multi-storey car park on the site of the old bus depot, which has been empty for years. Such a building would hold more cars on a smaller plot of land. Moreover, the depot is just outside the town centre, so commuters could park there and walk to work. This would not only solve the parking problem but also reduce traffic in the centre.

In short, the park is worth far more than a few hundred parking spaces. I would be grateful if you could publish my letter, as I hope it will encourage other residents to make their voices heard before the final decision is made.
Yours faithfully,
Marta Zielińska

paragraphs: Dear Sir or Madam,

As a member of the drama group at the Youth Cultural Centre, I was shocked to learn that the council intends to close the centre next year to cut costs. I am writing to ask you to reconsider this decision.

Last spring, the centre organised a three-day theatre festival for secondary school students from across the region. Our group spent two months preparing a play based on stories collected from our grandparents. On the final evening, the hall was so full that people stood at the back, and afterwards several elderly residents told us how moved they were. For most of us, it was the first time we had performed in front of a real audience.

I fully understand that the town has to reduce its spending. However, closing the centre would be a false economy, as the town would lose far more than it would save. The centre offers low-cost activities to over three hundred young people every week, many of whom cannot afford private lessons. Without it, they would have nowhere to go after school except shopping centres. Furthermore, it brings different generations together through events like our festival, which no other place in town does.

For these reasons, I urge the council to look for savings elsewhere and keep the centre open. I would also be grateful if you could meet some of the young people who use the centre before a final decision is made.
Yours faithfully,
Jakub Malinowski

paragraphs: Dear Ms Kowalczyk,

Thank you for asking students for their opinions on the planned ban on mobile phones. I am writing to share the views of my class. While we agree that phones cause problems at our school, we believe that a total ban is not the best solution and would like to propose an alternative.

At present, phones are part of almost every moment of the school day. Many students use them for sensible purposes, such as checking changes to the timetable, looking up words in English lessons or contacting their parents. However, during breaks most of us simply stare at our screens instead of talking to each other, and the corridors have become strangely quiet. Some students also play games in class, which distracts everyone around them.

Instead of a complete ban, we would suggest that the school introduce two simple rules. Firstly, phones should stay in our bags during lessons unless a teacher asks us to use them. Secondly, the lunch break could be phone-free, with board games and table tennis available in the hall. Such rules would be easier to enforce than a total ban, and they would teach us to control our phone use ourselves.
We are convinced that students would respect rules they have helped to create. We would be grateful if you could discuss this proposal with the student council before the final decision is made.
Yours sincerely,
Zuzanna Lis

paragraphs: Hello,

My name is Kasia and I am seventeen years old. I live in a small village near the town and I go to school by bus every day. I read your article about the buses and I want to write what I think about it.

It's really bad for kids from villages like mine. Now there are a lot of buses, so I can choose. From September there will be only one bus in the morning and one in the afternoon. Students will must wake up at five o'clock and they will be very tired on lessons. After lessons we will have to wait two or three hours for the bus home, so a lot of students won't go to extra classes or sports clubs beacause they won't have time. Some parents can drive their kids, but not everybody has a car and my parents work in another town.

I am agree that the bus company must to save money. They can use smaller buses or something. In the afternoon there are not many people on the bus anyway. It will be cheaper and better for everybody. The authorities should do something because young people are the future.
I hope you liked my letter. Please answer me fast.
Best wishes,
Kasia

paragraphs: Dear Editor,

I am writing in response to your article on the planned cuts to bus services between the surrounding villages and the town. As a student who travels to school by bus every day, I am deeply concerned about this decision, and I would like to suggest a fairer way of saving money.

If the plan goes ahead, students like me will have to catch the only morning bus at around six o'clock, more than an hour before lessons begin. Getting up so early is bound to affect our concentration. The afternoon will be even worse. With just one bus after school, anyone who stays for extra classes or exam preparation will simply have no way of getting home. As a result, students from villages will be at a clear disadvantage compared with their classmates from the town.

Rather than cancelling most of the services, the bus company could replace its large buses with minibuses outside peak hours. A minibus uses considerably less fuel, so the savings would be significant, while students and elderly residents would still have several buses a day. In this way, the company would cut its costs without leaving anyone stranded.

To sum up, the cuts would save money in the short term, but they would also limit opportunities for young people in our area. I would be grateful if you could publish my letter, as I hope it will persuade the company to reconsider.
Yours faithfully,
Katarzyna Nowak
